chapter: Cab Calloway, Lunceford, Hampton and Armstrong, 1941-45
title: Coca-Cola broadcasts and precise timing
summary: The band did nineteen Coca-Cola shows, each timed exactly to the half hour with the producer cueing cuts through earphones.

story.theme_name: Working with and around Louis Armstrong
story.community_name: Playing with and around Louis Armstrong

blocks.x: I figured that at this time in Louie's life, he needed a little rest from all that brass.
Yeah.
And we were -- this band was built for leading up to these things we were gonna do like all those Coca-cola shows that we did.
We did nineteen of them. We had the highest record -- we did more than any other bands did on the Coca-cola. They liked it, you know.
S. & S. REPORTING COMPANY, INC. WOrth 2-2915 WOrth 2-2943
We seemed -- I had the band where we come off on a break on the news -- we go over the news overseas, come back.

It was quite a technical thing to do perfect. You had to do it perfect every time. And we got the best rating (inaudible), because I used to arrange the music, rehearse it, right precise and keep the tempos so we wouldn't be behind and wouldn't be ahead, or something like that.
In doing a coast to coast broadcast for a big company like that, Coca-cola, you have to -- everything have to be exact.
Like the producer would stand on the side and tell you when you're ahead, cut off this, go (inaudible), you know.
He would be talking to me in the earphones. Louie would be singing -- can you jump to the last chorus, thirty seconds behind, you know.
We're taking up too much time, (inaudible). We be playing. Louie would be singing something, then Louie would come out of the chorus, I bring my hand (inaudible) we'd jumped (inaudible) --
S. & S. REPORTING COMPANY, INC. WOrth 2-2915 WOrth 2-2943
Before Louie come back and we jump from where Louie was at right to the last chorus. I told (inaudible), let us so and so, (inaudible) a number -- jump and Louie be singing something.
When Louie come out of his singing chorus, instead of him -- the band continue, we just stop (singing notes), right to the last chorus.
That way, we pick up the time that we need. The guy would give me the round q of the fingers, okay, we're on time.
That was going right into overseas. You must hit that overseas twenty minutes after. We come back twenty-five of, play a short number into the theme song.
Everything had to be synchronized.
Everything had to be exact. And you worked that way.
Now, I know Hamp had a lot of trouble, because Hamp would be up there playing the boogies. And some of them would be over too long and they would cut him off and go right into the news thing.
S. & S. REPORTING COMPANY, INC. WOrth 2-2915 WOrth 2-2943
And here the band would still be playing. You know, they didn't want it that way. They wanted you to end up, go into the (inaudible).
Then the man would say, "Now we're going overseas to pick up the war news," you know. And this was the thing we did, because I worked out with the producer of the show.
They came out every week -- every other week -- when we played these Coca-cola shows, whether it's a Army base or Navy base -- and things like that.
And you have to rehearse these shows. And you have to produce it. Now, the producer wouldn't tell you what to do with your band, but he would tell you how much time you had.
And you have to rehearse your numbers and cut them down. If you was gonna do a long number, cut it down to the spot where you could get in a number of Louie, a number for Velma, and the band.
Then the break, come back, one number, and over to the overseas thing, see. In a half hour you must do a half hour show -- all the announcements and everything had to be worked -- everything had to
